title: Greetings come in pairs
summary: Most Arabic greetings have a fixed reply. Learn them as pairs.
formula: greeting → fixed reply
explanation: When someone says السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ (peace be upon you), the reply is وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ (and upon you be peace). صَبَاحُ الْخَيْر (morning of goodness) is answered with صَبَاحُ النُّور (morning of light). مَرْحَبًا (hello) is often answered with مَرْحَبًا or أَهْلًا. These are fixed phrases: say them exactly, even if you don't analyse every word yet.

head: Greeting
Reply
Meaning
rows: peace be upon you / and upon you be peace

title: I, you, he, she
summary: Arabic has a different word for 'you' when you speak to a man and to a woman.
formula: أَنَا I · أَنْتَ you (m) · أَنْتِ you (f) · هُوَ he · هِيَ she
explanation: The words look almost the same on paper: only the last vowel changes. أَنْتَ (anta) is for a man, أَنْتِ (anti) for a woman. Without harakat both are written أنت, so the vowel marks matter while you learn.

title: my, your: endings on the noun
summary: 'My' and 'your' are endings joined to the end of the noun.
formula: noun + ـِي (my) · ـُكَ (your, m) · ـُكِ (your, f)
explanation: اِسْم means 'name'. Add ـِي to get اِسْمِي (my name). Add ـُكَ when you talk to a man (اِسْمُكَ, your name) and ـُكِ when you talk to a woman (اِسْمُكِ). The ending is written joined to the word: never as a separate word.

examples.en: What is your name? (to a man)

title: No word for 'am / is / are'
summary: In the present tense, Arabic puts two words side by side without a verb 'to be'.
formula: subject + description  (أَنَا + مِصْرِيّ = I am Egyptian)
explanation: أَنَا مِصْرِيّ is literally 'I Egyptian'. The 'am' is understood. This kind of sentence, which starts with a noun or pronoun, is called a nominal sentence. Questions work the same way: أَيْنَ الْبَيْت؟ 'where (is) the house?'.

title: Nationality words: -ī and -iyya
summary: Add ـِيّ to a country to say a man's nationality, and ـِيَّة for a woman's.
formula: country + ـِيّ (m) · + ـِيَّة (f)
explanation: مِصْر (Egypt) → مِصْرِيّ (an Egyptian man) → مِصْرِيَّة (an Egyptian woman). Drop a final ā or the article first: لُبْنَان → لُبْنَانِيّ. The feminine adds ة, which you will meet on every feminine word.

title: Question words
summary: Question words go at the start of the sentence.
formula: question word + rest of the sentence + ؟
explanation: كَيْفَ (how), أَيْنَ (where), مَا (what, before a noun) and مَنْ (who) start the question. The Arabic question mark ؟ is a mirrored ?. For yes/no questions, put هَلْ at the start: هَلْ أَنْتَ مِصْرِيّ؟ (Are you Egyptian?).

title: this: هٰذَا and هٰذِهِ (gender)
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine. Use هٰذَا for masculine and هٰذِهِ for feminine.
formula: هٰذَا + masculine noun · هٰذِهِ + feminine noun
explanation: Most feminine nouns end in ة (a tied t): عَائِلَة, سَيَّارَة. Female people are feminine too, with or without ة: أُمّ (mother), بِنْت (girl). Note the small upright alif in هٰذَا and هٰذِهِ: it is a long ā that is not written as a full letter.

head: Masculine
Feminine
English
rows: this is a father / this is a mother
this is a brother / this is a sister
this is a book / this is a car

title: the: الـ (al-)
summary: 'The' is الـ joined to the front of the noun. There is no word for 'a'.
formula: الـ + noun  (كِتَاب a book → الْكِتَاب the book)
explanation: A noun without الـ means 'a': كِتَاب = a book. With الـ it means 'the'. Before a sun letter the l is not said and the next letter is doubled (السَّيَّارَة as-sayyāra). Before a moon letter the l is said (الْقَلَم al-qalam).

title: Adjectives follow and agree
summary: An adjective comes after its noun and matches it in gender and in 'the'.
formula: noun + adjective (same gender, both with or both without الـ)
explanation: كِتَاب جَدِيد = a new book. سَيَّارَة جَدِيدَة = a new car (feminine adds ة to the adjective). الْكِتَاب الْجَدِيد = the new book. But الْكِتَاب جَدِيد (only the noun has الـ) is a sentence: the book is new.

title: Numbers 1–10
summary: Learn the counting forms 1–10 and the Arabic digits ١ to ١٠.
formula: ١ وَاحِد · ٢ اِثْنَان · ٣ ثَلَاثَة … ١٠ عَشَرَة
explanation: These are the forms used when counting and in phone numbers. Arabic digits are written left to right inside right-to-left text: ١٢ is twelve. With nouns, 3–10 have special rules that come later in the course.

examples.en: My number is five seven three.

title: Jobs for men and women
summary: A job word for a woman usually adds ة to the word for a man.
formula: مُدَرِّس (m) + ة → مُدَرِّسَة (f)
explanation: طَالِب is a male student and طَالِبَة a female student. Almost every job works the same way: مُهَنْدِس → مُهَنْدِسَة, طَبِيب → طَبِيبَة. Use the form that matches the person: هِيَ طَبِيبَة (she is a doctor). There is no word for 'a': أَنَا مُمَرِّض means 'I am a nurse'. To ask about a job, say مَا عَمَلُكَ؟ to a man and مَا عَمَلُكِ؟ to a woman.

title: Noun + noun: 'the … of …' (iḍāfa)
summary: Put two nouns side by side to say 'the X of Y': يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَة, Friday (literally 'the day of Friday').
formula: noun (no الـ) + noun with الـ, a name or a 'my/your' ending
explanation: In كِتَابُ دَانْيَال (Daniel's book) the first noun never takes الـ, yet it is definite: 'the book of Daniel'. The second noun is a name, a noun with الـ, or a noun with an ending such as ـِي. A ة at the end of the first noun is said as t: مَدْرَسَةُ اللُّغَة (madrasatu l-lugha, the language school). In careful speech the first noun carries a case vowel (often -u) and the second takes -i; at the end of a sentence the last vowel is usually dropped.

title: Telling the time
summary: Say السَّاعَة (the hour) and a feminine ordinal: السَّاعَة الثَّالِثَة, three o'clock.
formula: السَّاعَة + ordinal (f) + وَالرُّبْع / وَالنِّصْف / إِلَّا رُبْعًا
explanation: Ask كَمِ السَّاعَة؟ (what time is it?, literally 'how much is the hour?'). Answer with السَّاعَة and the feminine 'first, second, third…' word, because سَاعَة is feminine: السَّاعَة الْخَامِسَة (five o'clock). One o'clock is السَّاعَة الْوَاحِدَة. Add وَالرُّبْع (and a quarter), وَالنِّصْف (and a half) or إِلَّا رُبْعًا (minus a quarter). Add صَبَاحًا for the morning and مَسَاءً for the evening. 'At' a time is فِي: فِي السَّاعَة التَّاسِعَة (at nine o'clock).

title: The present tense: I, you, he, she
summary: A present-tense verb adds a prefix for the person: a- for I, ta- for you, ya- for he.
formula: a- (I) · ta- (you, m) · ta- … -īna (you, f) · ya- (he) · ta- (she) + stem + -u
explanation: Arabic verbs change at the front to show who is doing the action. Take ذَهَبَ (he went): أَذْهَبُ (I go), تَذْهَبُ (you go, to a man), تَذْهَبِينَ (you go, to a woman), يَذْهَبُ (he goes), تَذْهَبُ (she goes). 'You' (m) and 'she' look the same; the pronoun or the context tells them apart. The pronoun is usually left out, because the verb already shows the person: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَة means 'I go to school'. One present form covers 'I go', 'I am going' and 'I do go'.

title: We, you all, they: plural verbs
summary: With 'we' the prefix is na-; with 'you' (a group) and 'they' the verb also ends in -ūna.
formula: نَحْنُ نَدْرُسُ · أَنْتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ · هُمْ يَدْرُسُونَ
explanation: You already know أَدْرُسُ (I study) and يَدْرُسُ (he studies). For 'we', the prefix is na-: نَدْرُسُ (we study). For 'you' talking to a group, and for 'they', the verb takes a prefix and the ending ـُونَ: أَنْتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ (you study), هُمْ يَدْرُسُونَ (they study). أَنْتُمْ and هُمْ are used for groups of men and for mixed groups.

title: Not: لَا before a present verb
summary: Put لَا before a present-tense verb to say 'not': لَا أَعْرِفُ, I don't know.
formula: لَا + present verb
explanation: On its own لَا means 'no'. Before a present-tense verb it means 'not', and the verb itself does not change: أَفْهَمُ (I understand) → لَا أَفْهَمُ (I don't understand); يَعْمَلُ (he works) → لَا يَعْمَلُ (he doesn't work). English needs 'do' or 'does'; Arabic does not. لَا is only for verbs: to say 'I am not …' in a sentence without a verb, Arabic uses لَيْسَ, which comes in week 5.

title: Colours: masculine and feminine
summary: The basic colours have a masculine form like أَحْمَر and a feminine form like حَمْرَاء.
formula: m: aCCaC (أَحْمَر) · f: CaCCāʾ (حَمْرَاء)
explanation: The basic colours share one pattern. The masculine starts with أَ: أَحْمَر (red), أَزْرَق (blue). The feminine has a different shape ending in ـَاء: حَمْرَاء, زَرْقَاء. Like every adjective, a colour comes after its noun and matches it: قَلَم أَحْمَر (a red pen), سَيَّارَة حَمْرَاء (a red car). Some colours come from things and work like nationality words, with ـِيّ and ـِيَّة: بُنِّيّ, بُنِّيَّة (brown, from coffee beans).

title: The object ending -an
summary: The object of a verb takes the ending -a: -an (tanwīn) without 'the', a single -a with الـ.
formula: verb + object: آكُلُ خُبْزًا (I eat bread) · أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ (I drink tea)
explanation: In آكُلُ خُبْزًا (I eat bread), خُبْز is the object, the thing that is eaten, so it ends in -an. This ending is written as two fathas, usually with an extra alif: خُبْزًا, شَايًا. After ة there is no extra alif: قَهْوَةً. A word with الـ never has tanwīn, so a definite object ends in a single fatha: أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ. Arabic uses الـ for things in general, where English uses no article at all. In everyday speech, and at the end of a sentence, the ending is often not pronounced, but you will see it in careful writing.

examples.en: I eat bread and cheese for breakfast.
Do you drink tea or coffee? (to a woman)

title: Ordering politely: أُرِيدُ … مِنْ فَضْلِكَ
summary: Order with أُرِيدُ (I'd like) + the thing you want + 'please'. Ask what there is with هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ…؟
formula: أُرِيدُ + object (-an) + مِنْ فَضْلِكَ / مِنْ فَضْلِكِ
explanation: أُرِيدُ means 'I want', and with 'please' it is the normal polite way to order: أُرِيدُ شَايًا، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (I'd like a tea, please). 'Please' changes with the person you speak to: مِنْ فَضْلِكَ to a man, مِنْ فَضْلِكِ to a woman. لَوْ سَمَحْتَ / لَوْ سَمَحْتِ ('if you allow') is just as polite and is also how you catch a waiter's attention. To ask what a café has, say هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ…؟ (do you have…?). A cup or a bottle comes first, then the drink: فِنْجَانُ قَهْوَة (a cup of coffee), زُجَاجَةُ مَاء (a bottle of water). After أُرِيدُ the first word takes the object ending: أُرِيدُ فِنْجَانَ قَهْوَة.

examples.en: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.

examples.ar: أُرِيدُ شَايًا بِدُونِ سُكَّر، لَوْ سَمَحْتِ.
examples.en: I'd like a tea without sugar, please. (to a woman)

title: Sound plurals: -ūna and -āt
summary: Add ـُونَ for a group of men or a mixed group, and ـَات for women and many things. The singular stays whole.
formula: طَبَّاخ → طَبَّاخُونَ (-ūna) · سَلَطَة → سَلَطَات (-āt)
explanation: The masculine sound plural adds ـُونَ: طَبَّاخ (cook) → طَبَّاخُونَ (cooks), مِصْرِيّ → مِصْرِيُّونَ (Egyptians). After a verb or a preposition the ending becomes ـِينَ: شُكْرًا لِلطَّبَّاخِينَ (thanks to the cooks). It is used for people, and adjectives that describe male people take it too: طَبَّاخُونَ مُمْتَازُونَ. The feminine sound plural drops ة and adds ـَات: سَلَطَة → سَلَطَات, طَبَّاخَة → طَبَّاخَات. Many masculine words for things also take ـَات: مَشْرُوب → مَشْرُوبَات (drinks). Important: the plural of a thing takes a feminine singular adjective: مَشْرُوبَات بَارِدَة (cold drinks), سَلَطَات كَثِيرَة (many salads).

head: Singular
Plural
Rule
rows: after a verb or preposition: + ـِينَ

examples.en: The cooks in this restaurant are Egyptian.
We have salads and cold drinks.

title: Likes and dislikes: أُحِبُّ and يُعْجِبُنِي
summary: أُحِبُّ + الـ noun = I like (things in general take الـ). لَا أُحِبُّ = I don't like. With يُعْجِبُنِي the thing you like is the subject.
formula: (لَا) أُحِبُّ + الـ noun (-a) · يُعْجِبُنِي / تُعْجِبُنِي + الـ noun
explanation: أُحِبُّ means 'I like' and 'I love'. Something you like in general takes الـ, and as the object it ends in -a: أُحِبُّ الْقَهْوَةَ (I like coffee). For 'I don't like', put لَا directly before the verb: لَا أُحِبُّ الطَّعَامَ الْحَارَّ. To make it stronger, add كَثِيرًا (a lot) or, with a negative, أَبَدًا (at all). The verb changes with the person: أُحِبُّ (I), تُحِبُّ (you, to a man), تُحِبِّينَ (you, to a woman), يُحِبُّ (he), نُحِبُّ (we). A second way is يُعْجِبُنِي, literally 'it pleases me'. Here the food is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: يُعْجِبُنِي الْكُشَرِي (masculine), تُعْجِبُنِي الْقَهْوَة (feminine).

title: Broken plurals
summary: Most plurals change the vowels inside the word: كِتَاب → كُتُب, صَحْن → صُحُون. Plurals of things take a feminine singular adjective.
formula: same root letters, new vowel pattern: صَحْن → صُحُون · قَلَم → أَقْلَام
explanation: The root letters stay, but the vowels around them change: كِتَاب (book) → كُتُب, صَحْن (plate) → صُحُون, قَلَم (pen) → أَقْلَام, مِلْعَقَة (spoon) → مَلَاعِق. Some patterns are common (aCCāC, CuCūC, maCāCiC), but you cannot always guess the plural, so learn each noun with its plural. Two rules of agreement: (1) a plural of things counts as feminine singular, so it takes an adjective with ة and the pronoun هِيَ: الصُّحُون كَبِيرَة، هِيَ فِي الْمَطْبَخ. (2) A plural of people takes a plural adjective: أَصْدِقَاء كَثِيرُونَ (many friends). After the numbers three to ten the noun is plural: عَشَرَة أَرْغِفَة (ten loaves).

examples.en: Where are the spoons? They are in the kitchen.

title: The dual: exactly two
summary: For two of something add ـَانِ (subject, on its own) or ـَيْنِ (after a verb or preposition). ة becomes ت.
formula: كُوب → كُوبَانِ / كُوبَيْنِ · شَطِيرَة → شَطِيرَتَانِ / شَطِيرَتَيْنِ
explanation: Arabic has a special form for exactly two things or people, the dual. Add ـَانِ to the singular: كِتَاب → كِتَابَانِ (two books). After a verb or a preposition the ending is ـَيْنِ: أُرِيدُ كُوبَيْنِ (I'd like two glasses), مِنْ بَلَدَيْنِ (from two countries). A feminine ة is written as an open ت before the ending, and you hear the t: شَطِيرَة → شَطِيرَتَانِ. The dual already means 'two', so you normally don't add the number; اِثْنَانِ (m) or اِثْنَتَانِ (f) after the noun only adds emphasis. Adjectives agree and take the same ending: الْكُوبَانِ كَبِيرَانِ (the two glasses are big). To say 'two glasses of juice', use مِنْ: كُوبَانِ مِنَ الْعَصِير.

title: Numbers 11–100 and prices
summary: 11–19 are two words (خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ), the tens end in ـُونَ (ثَلَاثُونَ), and 21–99 are 'five and twenty'. After 11–99 the noun is singular with -an: عِشْرُونَ جُنَيْهًا.
formula: ١٥ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ · ٢٠ عِشْرُون · ٧٥ خَمْسَة وَسَبْعُونَ · ١٠٠ مِئَة
explanation: 11 is أَحَدَ عَشَرَ and 12 is اِثْنَا عَشَرَ. 13 to 19 are 'three-ten' to 'nine-ten': ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ, خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ. The tens add ـُونَ: عِشْرُون (20, the odd one out), ثَلَاثُون, أَرْبَعُون, خَمْسُون, سِتُّون, سَبْعُون, ثَمَانُون, تِسْعُون. Like the sound plural, they end in ـِينَ after a verb or a preposition: بِعِشْرِينَ (for twenty). From 21 to 99 the unit comes first, joined by وَ: خَمْسَة وَسَبْعُونَ is 'five and seventy', 75. 100 is مِئَة. The counted noun changes with the number: after 3–10 it is plural (ثَلَاثَة جُنَيْهَات), after 11–99 it is singular with the ending -an (عِشْرُونَ جُنَيْهًا), and after مِئَة it is singular (مِئَةُ جُنَيْه). These forms are for a masculine noun such as جُنَيْه; with feminine nouns some units change, which comes later in the course. To ask a price, say بِكَمْ؟ (for how much?).

title: Verb first: the verbal sentence
summary: A sentence that starts with a verb is a verbal sentence. Before its subject the verb stays singular, even when the subject is plural.
formula: verb + subject (+ object)  (يَزُورُ السُّيَّاحُ الْمَتْحَفَ = the tourists visit the museum)
explanation: Arabic often puts the verb first: يَذْهَبُ سَامِي إِلَى الْمَسْجِد (Sami goes to the mosque). The verb shows the gender of the subject: يَـ for a man or a masculine noun, تَـ for a woman or a feminine noun, as in تَذْهَبُ لَيْلَى (Layla goes). When the verb comes first it stays singular, even with a plural subject: يَزُورُ السُّيَّاحُ الْمَتْحَفَ, never يَزُورُونَ السُّيَّاحُ. In careful Arabic the subject ends in -u and the object in -a (as-suyyāḥu, al-matḥafa), but these endings are usually dropped at the end of a sentence.

examples.en: The tourists visit the museum every day.

title: First, second, third: ordinal numbers
summary: Ordinals are adjectives: they come after the noun and agree with it in gender and in 'the'.
formula: noun + ordinal  (الشَّارِع الثَّانِي the second street · الْبِنَايَة الثَّالِثَة the third building)
explanation: Apart from أَوَّل (first), the ordinals are built from the numbers on the pattern fāʿil: ثَلَاثَة (three) → الثَّالِث (the third), خَمْسَة (five) → الْخَامِس (the fifth). Like any adjective they follow the noun, take الـ when the noun has it, and add ة for a feminine noun: الْبِنَايَة الثَّالِثَة. The feminine of أَوَّل is irregular: الْأُولَى. أَوَّل can also stand in front of an indefinite noun: أَوَّلُ يَوْم (the first day).

examples.en: Take the second street on the right.
The bookshop is in the third building.

title: By bus, by taxi: bi-
summary: To say how you travel, join بِـ (by) to the vehicle with الـ. On foot is مَشْيًا.
formula: بِـ + الـ + vehicle  (بِالْمِتْرُو = by metro)
explanation: بِـ is a one-letter preposition, written joined to the next word. With the article it becomes bi-l-: بِالْحَافِلَة (by bus), بِالتَّاكْسِي (by taxi), بِالسَّيَّارَة (by car). The alif of الـ is still written but not said. For 'on foot' Arabic uses one word, مَشْيًا (walking). To take or ride a vehicle is يَرْكَبُ, with the vehicle straight after it and no preposition: يَرْكَبُ الطُّلَّابُ الْحَافِلَةَ (the students take the bus).

examples.en: I go to school by metro.
The students take the bus every morning.

title: Where things are: words of place
summary: Words like أَمَامَ (in front of) and خَلْفَ (behind) come straight before a noun, and that noun takes the ending -i.
formula: word of place + noun ending in -i  (خَلْفَ الْبَنْكِ = behind the bank)
explanation: Most words of place end in -a: أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ, فَوْقَ, تَحْتَ, بَيْنَ, مُقَابِلَ. The noun after them is in the genitive case, so it ends in -i: أَمَامَ الْمَدْرَسَةِ (in front of the school). In speech this -i is often dropped at the end of a sentence. With a pronoun ending they work like nouns: خَلْفَهُ (behind it), خَلْفَكَ (behind you). Don't confuse فِي (in, inside) with عَلَى (on top of).

examples.en: The post office is behind the bank.
The book is on the table.

title: There is, there are: hunāka
summary: Put هُنَاكَ before an indefinite noun to say 'there is' or 'there are'. Add هَلْ in front to ask.
formula: هُنَاكَ + noun without الـ  (هُنَاكَ صَيْدَلِيَّة = there is a pharmacy)
explanation: هُنَاكَ literally means 'there'. At the start of a sentence it introduces something new: هُنَاكَ بَنْك فِي هٰذَا الشَّارِع (there is a bank on this street). The same word works for one thing or many: هُنَاكَ مَحَلَّات كَثِيرَة (there are many shops). To ask, put هَلْ in front: هَلْ هُنَاكَ صَيْدَلِيَّة قَرِيبَة؟ (is there a pharmacy nearby?). For 'there isn't', say لَيْسَ هُنَاكَ. You can also start with the place: فِي الْمَدِينَة مَسَاجِد كَثِيرَة (in the city there are many mosques). Don't mix up هُنَاكَ (there) and هُنَا (here).

examples.en: There is a pharmacy near here.

examples.ar: هَلْ هُنَاكَ بَنْك فِي هٰذَا الشَّارِع؟
examples.en: Is there a bank on this street?

title: Plurals of things count as 'she'
summary: The plural of a thing or an animal is treated as feminine singular: it takes هٰذِهِ, هِيَ and an adjective with ة.
formula: plural of things + feminine singular adjective  (الْقُمْصَان جَمِيلَة = the shirts are beautiful)
explanation: Arabic sorts plurals into two groups. Plurals of people keep a plural adjective: الْبَاعَة لُطَفَاء (the sellers are kind). But the plural of anything that is not a person, such as shirts, streets, shops or lanterns, behaves like one feminine word: الشَّوَارِع مُزْدَحِمَة (the streets are crowded), هٰذِهِ الْأَحْذِيَة غَالِيَة (these shoes are expensive). You also refer to them with هِيَ (she, it), and a verb takes the feminine تَـ.

examples.en: The shops are open until ten.

title: There is…: put the place first
summary: To say what there is somewhere, start with the place: فِي الشَّقَّة شُرْفَة (there is a balcony in the flat).
formula: فِي + place + thing (no الـ)
explanation: Arabic needs no word for 'there is'. Put the place first and the thing after it, without الـ: فِي الشَّقَّة مَطْبَخ (in the flat, a kitchen = there is a kitchen in the flat). To ask, put هَلْ in front: هَلْ فِي الشَّقَّة شُرْفَة؟ If the thing has الـ, use the normal order instead: الْمَطْبَخ فِي الشَّقَّة (the kitchen is in the flat). Instead of naming the place again, use فِيهِ (in it, masculine) or فِيهَا (in it, feminine): الشَّقَّة صَغِيرَة، وَفِيهَا شُرْفَة.

examples.en: There is a bedroom and a kitchen in the flat.
There is a big window in the living room.

title: All the possessive endings
summary: Eight endings say whose something is: my, your (to a man, a woman, several people), his, her, our and their.
formula: noun + ـِي · ـُكَ · ـُكِ · ـُهُ · ـُهَا · ـُنَا · ـُكُمْ · ـُهُمْ
explanation: You already know ـِي (my), ـُكَ and ـُكِ (your), ـُهُ (his) and ـُهَا (her). Add ـُنَا (our), ـُكُمْ (your, to several people) and ـُهُمْ (their). Before any ending, ة turns into ت: غُرْفَة → غُرْفَتِي, غُرْفَتُنَا. After an i sound, ـُهُ and ـُهُمْ become ـِهِ and ـِهِمْ: لِعَائِلَتِهِ (for his family). A noun with an ending is already definite, so it never takes الـ as well. The same endings go on little words like عِنْدَ, مَعَ and فِي: عِنْدَهُ (he has), مَعَنَا (with us), فِيهَا (in it).

examples.en: This is my room, and this is my bed.

title: To have: عِنْدَ, لِـ and مَعَ
summary: Arabic has no verb 'to have'. It says 'at me', 'for me' or 'with me', using a possessive ending.
formula: عِنْدِي / لِي / مَعِي + thing (no الـ)
explanation: عِنْدِي سَيَّارَة is literally 'at me (is) a car', and it is the everyday way to say 'I have a car'. لِي (for me) is used above all for family and for what belongs to you: لِي أَخ وَأُخْت (I have a brother and a sister). مَعِي (with me) means you have something on you right now: مَعِي هَاتِفِي (I have my phone on me). Before an ending لِـ becomes لَـ: لَكَ, لَهُ, لَهَا, but لِي. To say you don't have something, put لَيْسَ in front: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي تِلْفَاز (I don't have a television).

examples.en: I have a new key for the flat.

title: Adjectives agree with their noun
summary: An adjective matches its noun in gender and in definiteness. A noun with an ending such as ـُهُ counts as definite.
formula: شَعْرُهُ الطَّوِيل = his long hair · شَعْرُهُ طَوِيل = his hair is long
explanation: On day 6 you met كِتَاب جَدِيد (a new book) and الْكِتَاب الْجَدِيد (the new book). A noun with a possessive ending is definite too, so an adjective that describes it takes الـ: شَعْرُهُ الطَّوِيل (his long hair). Without الـ the adjective says something about the noun, and you have a sentence: شَعْرُهُ طَوِيل (his hair is long). The adjective follows the gender of the noun, not of the owner: شَعْرُهَا طَوِيل (her hair is long), because شَعْر is masculine. For a group of people the adjective is plural: أَقَارِب كَثِيرُونَ (many relatives).

examples.en: Her hair is blond and long.
My little sister is very pretty.

title: is not: لَيْسَ
summary: لَيْسَ means 'is not'. It changes with the person, and the adjective after it ends in ـًا.
formula: لَيْسَ + adjective + ـًا  (هُوَ لَيْسَ طَوِيلًا)
explanation: Present-tense sentences have no word for 'is', but the negative does: لَيْسَ. It changes with the person like a verb: لَسْتُ (I am not), لَسْتَ and لَسْتِ (you are not), لَيْسَ (he is not), لَيْسَتْ (she is not), لَسْنَا (we are not). The adjective after it takes the accusative ending ـًا: هُوَ لَيْسَ طَوِيلًا. After ة the ending is ـَةً: هِيَ لَيْسَتْ طَوِيلَةً. In everyday speech this ending is often dropped, but write it. لَيْسَ also makes عِنْدِي negative: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي سَيَّارَة.

examples.en: Omar is not tall; he is short.

title: Saying your age
summary: Ask كَمْ عُمْرُكَ؟ and answer عُمْرِي + number + years. The word for 'years' depends on the number.
explanation: عُمْر means 'age' (and 'life'). Add an ending: عُمْرِي (my age), عُمْرُكَ, عُمْرُكِ, عُمْرُهُ, عُمْرُهَا. To ask, use كَمْ (how much): كَمْ عُمْرُكَ؟ After 3 to 10 comes the plural سَنَوَات, and because سَنَة is feminine the number loses its ة: عَشْرُ سَنَوَاتٍ (ten years), not عَشَرَة. From 11 upwards the singular follows, with the ending ـَةً: عِشْرُونَ سَنَةً. The round tens are easy: عِشْرُون, ثَلَاثُون, أَرْبَعُون, خَمْسُون, سِتُّون, سَبْعُون.

title: Family chains: اِبْنُ عَمِّي
summary: Put two family words side by side to say 'the son of my uncle'. Only the last word takes 'my' or الـ.
formula: first word (no الـ, ending ـُ) + second word + ending  (اِبْنُ عَمِّي)
explanation: Arabic links two nouns to say 'X of Y' with no word for 'of': اِبْنُ عَمِّي = son (of) my uncle = my cousin. The first word never takes الـ or a possessive ending, and its last vowel is usually ـُ. 'My' goes on the last word only: زَوْجَةُ خَالِي (my uncle's wife). The last word can also be a name: خَالَةُ سَامِي (Sami's aunt). When the first word ends in ة, it is said as t: زَوْجَةُ (zawjatu). Note that أَخ (brother) and أَب (father) become أَخُو and أَبُو before another word: أَخُو أَبِي (my father's brother).

examples.en: Khalid is my cousin (my mother's sister's son).
